rationale: B wins because it keeps closer to the supplied facts instead of trying to make Discord more dramatic than the update allows. A has sharper tailoring in places, but "Millions of Unpaid Gaming Community Managers Just Got a Business Model" is a credibility leak: "millions," "unpaid," and "just got" are not in the facts. B's "Discord undercuts Apple and Google, charging creators a 10% cut instead of 30%" is a cleaner reportable spine, and its refusal to manufacture a live antitrust peg shows actual editorial discipline.
gaps_in_A: "Discord's 10% Creator Cut Undercuts App Stores and Patreon" puts Patreon in the headline even though Patreon is not in the update and the comparison still needs proof.
"first real monetization product" is invented. The update says Discord is launching paid creator subscriptions, not that Discord lacks other revenue products.
"Millions of Unpaid Gaming Community Managers Just Got a Business Model" stacks three unsupported claims: millions, unpaid, and immediate business-model proof before any creator earnings exist.
"ongoing regulatory scrutiny of app store fees globally keeps this topic warm" may be true background, but it is not a supplied live peg. That is fake urgency with better tailoring.
gaps_in_B: "it won't say how much they'll make" implies Discord is withholding earnings data; the update only says no creator-earnings data exists yet because the program is new.

"how this revenue stream fits alongside existing lines (ads, Nitro)" imports outside revenue lines not supplied in the update. Asking for context is fine; naming unsupplied lines breaks the blind fact boundary.
"monetization is coming for the whole server, not just the streamer" is a good thought, but it needs proof of the streamer-vs-server contrast before it can carry the thesis.
"Decay: month" for the category angle is generous. One launch with no uptake data or comparable examples probably does not deserve a month-long pitch window.
